\chapter{Family}
\label{ch:ka-family}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name close family, refer to he, she, it or they, say who works, mark his, her or their, and make a familiar non-human noun plural.}

Name the family set, distinguish human from non-human third person, say who works, form his/her/their, and make \kn{ಹೆಸರು} and \kn{ಬಣ್ಣ} plural with -\kn{ಗಳು}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\kn{ಅಪ್ಪ} \kn{ಅಮ್ಮ} \kn{ಅಣ್ಣ} \kn{ತಮ್ಮ} … (appa amma aṇṇa …)}{ಅಪ್ಪ ಅಮ್ಮ ಅಣ್ಣ ತಮ್ಮ … (appa amma aṇṇa …)}]{\kn{ಅಪ್ಪ}, \kn{ಅಮ್ಮ}, and four sibling words — the same system as Tamil}

\label{lesson:KA-C12-kutumba}



\begin{quote}
Kannada asks the same question Tamil does about any sibling: \textbf{older, or younger?} — and the words for answering it are almost identical.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅಪ್ಪ}} (\emph{appa}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{father}\textquotedblright{} — matches Tamil \emph{appā} closely.
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅಮ್ಮ}} (\emph{amma}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{mother}\textquotedblright{} — matches Tamil \emph{ammā} closely.
\end{itemize}

Both are native Dravidian words (DEDR 156, 183).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Kannada} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{compare Tamil} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\kn{ಅಣ್ಣ}} (\emph{aṇṇa}) & \textbf{older} brother & \emph{aṇṇaṉ} — near match \\
\textbf{\kn{ತಮ್ಮ}} (\emph{tamma}) & \textbf{younger} brother & \emph{tambi} — near match \\
\textbf{\kn{ಅಕ್ಕ}} (\emph{akka}) & \textbf{older} sister & \emph{akkā} — near match \\
\textbf{\kn{ತಂಗಿ}} (\emph{tangi}) & \textbf{younger} sister & \emph{tangai} — near match \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

All four are native Dravidian, each with its own entry (DEDR 131, 3085, 23, 3015).

Just like Tamil, Kannada has \textbf{no single word} that simply means \textquotedblleft{}brother\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}sister\textquotedblright{} — you name the sibling's \textbf{relative age} every time, not just their gender. This age-first system runs across the whole Dravidian family, not just one language.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}appa, amma\textquotedblright{} — father, mother
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}aṇṇa, tamma\textquotedblright{} — older/younger brother
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}akka, tangi\textquotedblright{} — older/younger sister
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dayaviṭṭu}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\kn{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many Kannada sibling words are there, and what do they split on? (\textbf{Four} — \kn{ಅಣ್ಣ}/\kn{ತಮ್ಮ}, \kn{ಅಕ್ಕ}/\kn{ತಂಗಿ} — split by \textbf{relative age}, not just gender.) How closely do Kannada's words match Tamil's? (\textbf{Very closely} — nearly the same forms across the whole set.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\kn{ಅವನು} \kn{ಅವಳು} \kn{ಅದು} \kn{ಅವರು} (avanu avaḷu adu …)}{ಅವನು ಅವಳು ಅದು ಅವರು (avanu avaḷu adu …)}]{\kn{ಅವನು}, \kn{ಅವಳು}, \kn{ಅದು}, \kn{ಅವರು} — people and things outside the conversation}

\label{lesson:KA-C12-third-person}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\kn{ನಾನು}} for “I”, then name father, mother, older brother and older sister. Now point away from “I” and “you”: this lesson gives those people their pronouns.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: four third-person forms}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅವನು}} (\emph{avanu}) — he
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅವಳು}} (\emph{avaḷu}) — she
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅದು}} (\emph{adu}) — it, that non-human thing
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅವರು}} (\emph{avaru}) — they; also respectful “he” or “she”
\end{itemize}

Use \textbf{\kn{ಅವರು}} for one respected adult as well as for several people. The sentence around it tells you whether it means respectful singular or plural.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the first split is human or non-human}]
Kannada does not make every noun carry masculine or feminine marking. In the third person, the useful first question is \textbf{human or non-human}: \textbf{\kn{ಅವನು} / \kn{ಅವಳು} / \kn{ಅವರು}} point to people; \textbf{\kn{ಅದು}} points to a non-human thing. That split will matter again when verbs and plurals change shape.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} father, then “he” — \textbf{\kn{ಅಪ್ಪ}, \kn{ಅವನು}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} mother, then “she” — \textbf{\kn{ಅಮ್ಮ}, \kn{ಅವಳು}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\kn{ಅವರು}} once for “they”, then once for one respected adult
  \item \emph{Identify:} which one is non-human? — \textbf{\kn{ಅದು}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say he, she, it and they/respectful he or she. Which three forms point to people, and which one points to a non-human thing?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\kn{ಮಾಡುತ್ತಾನೆ} … (māḍuttāne …)}{ಮಾಡುತ್ತಾನೆ … (māḍuttāne …)}]{\kn{ಮಾಡುತ್ತಾನೆ}, \kn{ಮಾಡುತ್ತಾಳೆ}, \kn{ಮಾಡುತ್ತಾರೆ} — let the ending name the person}

\label{lesson:KA-C12-present-endings}



\begin{quote}
Say “I work”: \emph{nānu kelasa māḍuttēne}. Then say he, she and they/respectful he or she. Keep \emph{māḍutt-} still and change only the ending.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the ending follows the human pronoun}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{avanu kelasa māḍuttāne.} — He works.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{avaḷu kelasa māḍuttāḷe.} — She works.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{avaru kelasa māḍuttāre.} — They work; or one respected person works.
\end{quote}

The stem and \emph{-utt-} stay still. The endings \emph{-tāne, -tāḷe, -tāre} tell you which human pronoun fits. Keep the non-human present ending for a later lesson; for now, recognise \emph{adu} as the non-human member of the pronoun set.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} “He works” — \emph{avanu kelasa māḍuttāne}
  \item \emph{Say it:} “She works” — \emph{avaḷu kelasa māḍuttāḷe}
  \item \emph{Say it:} “They work” — \emph{avaru kelasa māḍuttāre}
  \item \emph{Identify:} which ending can also belong to one respected person? — \emph{-tāre}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Hold \emph{māḍutt-} still and give the three human endings: he, she, and they/respectful singular.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\kn{ಸ} (sa)}{ಸ (sa)}]{\kn{ಸ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S121-letter-sa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಹ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಸ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಸ}} — \emph{sa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{s}, it is \textbf{sa}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ಸ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}} \emph{namaskāra} — hello / greetings (namaskāra — \textquotedblleft{}a making of a bow\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಸರಿ}} \emph{sari} — okay / alright / correct (sari)
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹೆಸರು}} \emph{hesaru} — name
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}} \emph{santōṣa} — joy / pleased to meet you
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಸ}}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/KA-S121-letter-sa-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \kn{ಸ} is written, stroke by stroke}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the tail and climb round the left curve
  \item \textbf{2.} without lifting, slant down to the right into the base
  \item \textbf{3.} without lifting, climb the right side and curve in at the top
  \item \textbf{4.} lift, then draw the top bar from left to right
  \item \textbf{5.} without lifting, curl up into the hook
  \item \textbf{6.} lift, then set the dot in the middle
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The body is one run, from the tail at the bottom left to the curl at the top right; then comes the curled bar, and last the dot in the middle, each after a lift.

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — Kannada handwriting is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Gopala Krishna A, 'Kannada-alphabet-sa.gif', 40 frames, Wikimedia Commons, 25 May 2016, CC BY-SA 4.0.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ಸ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}  ·  \kn{ಸರಿ}  ·  \kn{ಧನ್ಯವಾದ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಸ} three times, saying \emph{sa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ಸ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಸ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{sa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\kn{ಅವನ} \kn{ಅವಳ} \kn{ಅವರ} (avana avaḷa avara)}{ಅವನ ಅವಳ ಅವರ (avana avaḷa avara)}]{\kn{ಅವನ}, \kn{ಅವಳ}, \kn{ಅವರ} — whose family member?}

\label{lesson:KA-C12-third-person-possession}



\begin{quote}
Say he, she and they/respectful he or she. Then say father, mother, older brother and older sister. Now join each person to a family word.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: remove the final pronoun ending}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅವನ} \kn{ಅಪ್ಪ}} (\emph{avana appa}) — his father
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅವಳ} \kn{ಅಮ್ಮ}} (\emph{avaḷa amma}) — her mother
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಅವರ} \kn{ಅಕ್ಕ}} (\emph{avara akka}) — their older sister, or a respected person's older sister
\end{itemize}

For this small set, hear the pair: \textbf{\kn{ಅವನು} $\to$ \kn{ಅವನ}}, \textbf{\kn{ಅವಳು} $\to$ \kn{ಅವಳ}}, \textbf{\kn{ಅವರು} $\to$ \kn{ಅವರ}}. This lesson teaches those three possessive forms as a set; it does not yet turn the ending into a rule for every noun.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} “his father” — \textbf{\kn{ಅವನ} \kn{ಅಪ್ಪ}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} “her mother” — \textbf{\kn{ಅವಳ} \kn{ಅಮ್ಮ}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} “their older sister” — \textbf{\kn{ಅವರ} \kn{ಅಕ್ಕ}}
  \item \emph{Identify:} which possessive can also belong to one respected person? — \textbf{\kn{ಅವರ}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Change he, she and they/respectful singular into his, her and their/respectful singular possessive.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\kn{೪} (4)}{೪ (4)}]{\kn{೪} — the digit for nālku}

\label{lesson:KA-S143-digit-four}



\begin{quote}
Before the new shape: \textbf{\kn{೩}} — which number is it?

One digit this time, and you already know its name.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{೪}}
\textbf{\kn{೪}} — \textbf{4}, the digit for \textbf{\kn{ನಾಲ್ಕು}} (\emph{nālku}), \textquotedblleft{}four\textquotedblright{}.

You have now met four of the ten. The words came first, when you learned to count; the shapes are arriving one at a time, on top of words you can already say.

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{೪} — follow the numbered strip}
\hlblockfigure{\detokenize{figures/KA-S143-digit-four-filmstrip.pdf}}{How \kn{೪} is written, stroke by stroke}

Follow the numbered strip: start where movement 1 begins, and let each panel show you the next movement before your pen makes it. Then write \kn{೪} yourself — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
The strip shows \textbf{where to start the character and which way to travel}, in one attested order. That is taught with real variation from school to school, so the strip names its source beneath it: treat it as a sound way in, not the only one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at the digits you have met, and name each one aloud
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{೧}  ·  \kn{೨}  ·  \kn{೩}  ·  \kn{೪}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}nālku\textquotedblright{} as you point at \kn{೪}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which number is \textbf{\kn{೪}}? (\textbf{4} — \emph{nālku}, \kn{ನಾಲ್ಕು}.) Name every digit you have met so far, in order.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\texorpdfstring{\kn{ಹೆಸರುಗಳು} \kn{ಬಣ್ಣಗಳು} (hesarugaḷu bannagaḷu)}{ಹೆಸರುಗಳು ಬಣ್ಣಗಳು (hesarugaḷu bannagaḷu)}]{\kn{ಹೆಸರುಗಳು}, \kn{ಬಣ್ಣಗಳು} — more than one non-human thing}

\label{lesson:KA-C12-plural-galu}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{\kn{ಹೆಸರು}}, “name”, then the four colours. These are non-human things, so their ordinary plural can use one ending.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: add -\kn{ಗಳು}}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹೆಸರು}} (\emph{hesaru}, name) $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ಹೆಸರುಗಳು}} (\emph{hesarugaḷu}, names)
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಬಣ್ಣ}} (\emph{banna}, colour) $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ಬಣ್ಣಗಳು}} (\emph{bannagaḷu}, colours)
\end{itemize}

The ending is \textbf{-\kn{ಗಳು}} (\emph{-gaḷu}). Use it here for ordinary non-human nouns. Do not force it onto the family words: human plurals have their own patterns, and \emph{avaru} already gives you “they” for people.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} “names” — \textbf{\kn{ಹೆಸರುಗಳು}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} “colours” — \textbf{\kn{ಬಣ್ಣಗಳು}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} “Her mother works” — \emph{avaḷa amma kelasa māḍuttāḷe}
  \item \emph{Identify:} which pronoun means people in the plural? — \emph{avaru}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Make “name” and “colour” plural. Then say “Her mother works.” Which pronoun gives you “they” for people?
\end{tcolorbox}
